Forecasting the Colour of the Year with Machine Learning¶

A time-series study of Pantone® Colours of the Year (2000–2026), industry colour forecasts and a century of decade palettes¶

Authors: Claude (Anthropic) · David Aguilar · Camila Gómez

This notebook is fully reproducible and is organised in three parts:

Part Content
A. Analysis Data collection → colour science (HEX, RGB, CMYK, HSV, CIELAB, LCh, harmonies) → Excel database with swatches → chromatic circle → walk-forward back-testing of 17 forecasting models → three-option forecast for 2027 → critique of the models and the method
B. Paper (English) Elsevier-style article describing the study and the forecast
C. Artículo (Español) Spanish version of the paper

Status of the target: as of 12 October 2026, Pantone has not announced its Colour of the Year 2027 (it is traditionally revealed in early December). Several paint brands have already announced their 2027 colours, and these are used as leading indicators.

Outputs generated by running this notebook

  • data/color_database.xlsx – the full colour database with real colour swatches painted in the cells (one sheet per series, harmonies, back-test results and the 2027 forecast).
  • data/color_database.csv – the same database in plain text.
  • figures/*.png – all figures used in the paper.

A.0 Setup¶

Run pip install -r requirements.txt once. Everything else is standard scientific Python.

A.1 Data collection¶

Three families of colour series were collected (October 2026). Every record keeps its source so that the database can be audited.

  1. Pantone® Colour of the Year (2000–2026) – the longest validated annual series of a "colour in fashion" and therefore the main forecasting target. Names, Pantone TCX codes and sRGB HEX approximations follow the table published by W3Schools (Colors Trends), cross-checked against Pantone press material. 2016 and 2021 had two colours each.
  2. Industry Colours of the Year – Sherwin-Williams (2011–2027), Benjamin Moore (2012–2026) and Behr (2019–2027), plus every other 2027 announcement with a published HEX (Valspar, Dulux, Glidden/PPG, Dutch Boy, Dunn-Edwards). Paint brands announce between August and October, before Pantone (December), so they are legitimate leading indicators. HEX values come from the brands' own colour libraries (via the MIT-licensed colornerd dataset) or the brands' 2027 press pages.
  3. Decade palettes (1920s–2020s) – historical literature on the dominant colours of each decade (Color-Meanings "History of colour by decade", Dunn-Edwards "Popular colour palettes through the decades", Juicebox Interactive). These texts give names, not codes, so each name was mapped to its standard named-colour HEX (e.g. Harvest Gold #DA9100, Avocado #568203). They are flagged approximate and used only for long-memory analysis (one observation per decade), never as forecasting targets.

A.2 Colour science toolkit¶

Every colour is described in several spaces:

  • HEX / RGB (sRGB) – what screens display.
  • CMYK – naive device-independent conversion (cyan, magenta, yellow, key/black), useful for print intuition but not a substitute for an ICC-profiled conversion.
  • HSV / HSL – hue-saturation models; the HSV hue wheel is used to build classical harmonies (complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary).
  • CIELAB (L*, a*, b*) and LCh – a perceptually uniform space (D65 white). All models are trained in CIELAB, and errors are measured with CIEDE2000 (ΔE₀₀), the industry-standard colour-difference formula. As a rule of thumb, ΔE₀₀ ≈ 1 is just noticeable, ≈ 10 is "clearly a different shade", and > 30 is "a different colour family".
In [3]:
# ============================== conversions ==================================
def hex_to_rgb(h):
    # '#RRGGBB' -> (R, G, B) integers 0-255
    h = h.lstrip("#")
    return tuple(int(h[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))

def rgb_to_hex(rgb):
    # (R, G, B) -> '#RRGGBB' (values are clipped to 0-255)
    r, g, b = [int(round(min(255, max(0, v)))) for v in rgb]
    return f"#{r:02X}{g:02X}{b:02X}"

def rgb_to_cmyk(rgb):
    # Naive RGB -> CMYK (percentages). Real print work needs an ICC profile.
    r, g, b = [v / 255 for v in rgb]
    k = 1 - max(r, g, b)
    if k >= 1:
        return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 100.0)
    c, m, y = [(1 - v - k) / (1 - k) for v in (r, g, b)]
    return tuple(round(100 * v, 1) for v in (c, m, y, k))

def _srgb_to_linear(c):
    c = np.asarray(c, float) / 255
    return np.where(c <= 0.04045, c / 12.92, ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)

def _linear_to_srgb(c):
    c = np.clip(c, 0, 1)
    return 255 * np.where(c <= 0.0031308, 12.92 * c, 1.055 * c ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055)

_M_RGB2XYZ = np.array([[0.4124564, 0.3575761, 0.1804375],
                       [0.2126729, 0.7151522, 0.0721750],
                       [0.0193339, 0.1191920, 0.9503041]])
_M_XYZ2RGB = np.linalg.inv(_M_RGB2XYZ)
_WHITE_D65 = np.array([0.95047, 1.00000, 1.08883])

def rgb_to_lab(rgb):
    # sRGB (0-255) -> CIELAB (D65 / 2 degree observer)
    xyz = _M_RGB2XYZ @ _srgb_to_linear(rgb) / _WHITE_D65
    f = np.where(xyz > (6 / 29) ** 3, np.cbrt(xyz), xyz / (3 * (6 / 29) ** 2) + 4 / 29)
    return np.array([116 * f[1] - 16, 500 * (f[0] - f[1]), 200 * (f[1] - f[2])])

def lab_to_rgb(lab):
    # CIELAB -> sRGB (0-255); out-of-gamut colours are clipped
    L, a, b = lab
    fy = (L + 16) / 116
    f = np.array([fy + a / 500, fy, fy - b / 200])
    xyz = np.where(f > 6 / 29, f ** 3, 3 * (6 / 29) ** 2 * (f - 4 / 29)) * _WHITE_D65
    return _linear_to_srgb(_M_XYZ2RGB @ xyz)

def lab_to_hex(lab):
    return rgb_to_hex(lab_to_rgb(lab))

def hex_to_lab(h):
    return rgb_to_lab(hex_to_rgb(h))

def lab_to_lch(lab):
    L, a, b = lab
    return np.array([L, math.hypot(a, b), math.degrees(math.atan2(b, a)) % 360])

def lch_to_lab(lch):
    L, C, h = lch
    return np.array([L, C * math.cos(math.radians(h)), C * math.sin(math.radians(h))])

# ============================ CIEDE2000 ======================================
def delta_e2000(lab1, lab2, kL=1, kC=1, kH=1):
    # CIEDE2000 colour difference (Luo, Cui & Rigg 2001; Sharma, Wu & Dalal 2005)
    L1, a1, b1 = lab1; L2, a2, b2 = lab2
    C1, C2 = math.hypot(a1, b1), math.hypot(a2, b2)
    Cbar = (C1 + C2) / 2
    G = 0.5 * (1 - math.sqrt(Cbar ** 7 / (Cbar ** 7 + 25 ** 7)))
    a1p, a2p = (1 + G) * a1, (1 + G) * a2
    C1p, C2p = math.hypot(a1p, b1), math.hypot(a2p, b2)
    h1p = math.degrees(math.atan2(b1, a1p)) % 360 if C1p else 0.0
    h2p = math.degrees(math.atan2(b2, a2p)) % 360 if C2p else 0.0
    dLp, dCp = L2 - L1, C2p - C1p
    dh = h2p - h1p
    if C1p * C2p == 0: dh = 0
    elif dh > 180: dh -= 360
    elif dh < -180: dh += 360
    dHp = 2 * math.sqrt(C1p * C2p) * math.sin(math.radians(dh / 2))
    Lbp, Cbp = (L1 + L2) / 2, (C1p + C2p) / 2
    if C1p * C2p == 0: hbp = h1p + h2p
    elif abs(h1p - h2p) <= 180: hbp = (h1p + h2p) / 2
    elif h1p + h2p < 360: hbp = (h1p + h2p + 360) / 2
    else: hbp = (h1p + h2p - 360) / 2
    T = (1 - 0.17 * math.cos(math.radians(hbp - 30)) + 0.24 * math.cos(math.radians(2 * hbp))
         + 0.32 * math.cos(math.radians(3 * hbp + 6)) - 0.20 * math.cos(math.radians(4 * hbp - 63)))
    dtheta = 30 * math.exp(-((hbp - 275) / 25) ** 2)
    Rc = 2 * math.sqrt(Cbp ** 7 / (Cbp ** 7 + 25 ** 7))
    Sl = 1 + 0.015 * (Lbp - 50) ** 2 / math.sqrt(20 + (Lbp - 50) ** 2)
    Sc, Sh = 1 + 0.045 * Cbp, 1 + 0.015 * Cbp * T
    Rt = -math.sin(math.radians(2 * dtheta)) * Rc
    return math.sqrt((dLp / (kL * Sl)) ** 2 + (dCp / (kC * Sc)) ** 2 + (dHp / (kH * Sh)) ** 2
                     + Rt * (dCp / (kC * Sc)) * (dHp / (kH * Sh)))

# Validation against the published test pairs of Sharma, Wu & Dalal (2005)
_tests = [((50, 2.6772, -79.7751), (50, 0, -82.7485), 2.0425),
          ((50, 3.1571, -77.2803), (50, 0, -82.7485), 2.8615),
          ((50, 2.8361, -74.0200), (50, 0, -82.7485), 3.4412),
          ((50, 0.0, 0.0),         (50, -1, 2),        2.3669)]
for l1, l2, ref in _tests:
    assert abs(delta_e2000(l1, l2) - ref) < 1e-3, (l1, l2, delta_e2000(l1, l2), ref)
print("CIEDE2000 implementation validated against Sharma et al. (2005) test data ✓")

# ======================= hue families and harmonies ==========================
# Hue sectors on the CIELAB hue circle, calibrated so that names match perception
# (e.g. sRGB pure blue sits at h = 306 deg in CIELAB, so 'Blue' spans 215-285 deg).
HUE_SECTORS = [(0, 30, "Red"), (30, 50, "Red-Orange/Coral"), (50, 80, "Orange/Amber"), (80, 105, "Yellow"),
               (105, 135, "Yellow-Green"), (135, 175, "Green"), (175, 215, "Teal/Cyan"), (215, 285, "Blue"),
               (285, 300, "Blue-Violet"), (300, 325, "Violet"), (325, 360, "Magenta/Pink")]
COARSE = {"Red": "Red", "Red-Orange/Coral": "Orange/Earth", "Orange/Amber": "Orange/Earth", "Brown/Earth": "Orange/Earth",
          "Yellow": "Yellow", "Yellow-Green": "Green", "Green": "Green", "Teal/Cyan": "Blue", "Blue": "Blue",
          "Blue-Violet": "Purple/Pink", "Violet": "Purple/Pink", "Magenta/Pink": "Purple/Pink"}
COARSE_FAMILIES = ["Red", "Orange/Earth", "Yellow", "Green", "Blue", "Purple/Pink", "Neutral"]

def hue_family(lab):
    # Fine family from CIELAB hue; low chroma -> Neutral; muted warm darks -> Brown/Earth
    L, C, h = lab_to_lch(lab)
    if C < 12:
        return "Neutral (white/grey)" if L > 35 else "Neutral (dark)"
    if 20 <= h < 90 and C < 45 and L < 65:
        return "Brown/Earth"
    return next(name for lo, hi, name in HUE_SECTORS if lo <= h < hi)

def coarse_family(lab):
    # 7 coarse classes used for classification metrics
    fam = hue_family(lab)
    return "Neutral" if fam.startswith("Neutral") else COARSE[fam]

def rotate_hue_hex(h, degrees):
    # rotate the HSV hue of a HEX colour (classical colour-wheel harmonies)
    r, g, b = [v / 255 for v in hex_to_rgb(h)]
    hh, s, v = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(r, g, b)
    return rgb_to_hex([255 * x for x in colorsys.hsv_to_rgb((hh + degrees / 360) % 1, s, v)])

def harmonies(h):
    return {"complementary": rotate_hue_hex(h, 180),
            "analogous_1": rotate_hue_hex(h, -30), "analogous_2": rotate_hue_hex(h, 30),
            "triadic_1": rotate_hue_hex(h, 120), "triadic_2": rotate_hue_hex(h, 240),
            "split_comp_1": rotate_hue_hex(h, 150), "split_comp_2": rotate_hue_hex(h, 210)}

print(hue_family(hex_to_lab("#0F4C81")), "|", harmonies("#0F4C81")["complementary"])

# ===================== build the master colour database ======================
def describe(hex_code):
    # Return every colour-space representation of one HEX colour as a dict
    rgb = hex_to_rgb(hex_code)
    lab = rgb_to_lab(rgb)
    L, C, h = lab_to_lch(lab)
    hh, s, v = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(*[x / 255 for x in rgb])
    hl, l2, s2 = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(*[x / 255 for x in rgb])
    c_, m_, y_, k_ = rgb_to_cmyk(rgb)
    d = {"hex": hex_code.upper(), "R": rgb[0], "G": rgb[1], "B": rgb[2],
         "C_cmyk": c_, "M_cmyk": m_, "Y_cmyk": y_, "K_cmyk": k_,
         "H_hsv": round(hh * 360, 1), "S_hsv": round(s * 100, 1), "V_hsv": round(v * 100, 1),
         "H_hsl": round(hl * 360, 1), "S_hsl": round(s2 * 100, 1), "L_hsl": round(l2 * 100, 1),
         "L_lab": round(lab[0], 2), "a_lab": round(lab[1], 2), "b_lab": round(lab[2], 2),
         "C_lch": round(C, 2), "h_lch": round(h, 1),
         "family": hue_family(lab), "coarse_family": coarse_family(lab)}
    d.update(harmonies(hex_code))
    return d

A.3 Excel database with real colour swatches¶

Each row of the workbook has its cell painted with the actual colour, plus the harmonies (complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary) painted next to it. Later cells append the back-test results and the 2027 forecast to the same workbook.

In [5]:
from openpyxl import Workbook
from openpyxl.styles import PatternFill, Font, Alignment
from openpyxl.utils import get_column_letter

def _text_color(hex_code):
    # black or white text depending on luminance, so labels stay readable on swatches
    return "000000" if rgb_to_lab(hex_to_rgb(hex_code))[0] > 55 else "FFFFFF"

def write_sheet(wb, title, df, swatch_cols=("hex",), widths=None):
    # Write a DataFrame to a sheet; every column listed in swatch_cols is painted with its own HEX value
    ws = wb.create_sheet(title)
    ws.append(list(df.columns))
    for c in ws[1]:
        c.font = Font(bold=True, color="FFFFFF"); c.fill = PatternFill("solid", fgColor="333333")
        c.alignment = Alignment(horizontal="center", vertical="center", wrap_text=True)
    for row in df.itertuples(index=False):
        ws.append([None if (isinstance(v, float) and np.isnan(v)) else v for v in row])
    cols = list(df.columns)
    for sc in swatch_cols:
        if sc not in cols: continue
        j = cols.index(sc) + 1
        for i in range(2, ws.max_row + 1):
            cell = ws.cell(i, j); v = cell.value
            if isinstance(v, str) and v.startswith("#") and len(v) == 7:
                cell.fill = PatternFill("solid", fgColor=v[1:])
                cell.font = Font(color=_text_color(v), bold=True)
    for j, col in enumerate(cols, 1):
        base_w = {"series": 16, "code": 18, "name": 22, "brand": 18, "source": 50, "reference_colour": 34,
                  "industry_members": 40, "hue_from": 50, "pantone_analogues": 50, "model": 26, "method": 30}
        base_w.update(widths or {})
        ws.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(j)].width = base_w.get(col, max(10, min(28, len(str(col)) + 4)))
    ws.freeze_panes = "A2"
    return ws

HARM = ["complementary", "analogous_1", "analogous_2", "triadic_1", "triadic_2", "split_comp_1", "split_comp_2"]
CORE_COLS = ["series", "year", "rank", "brand", "name", "code", "hex", "R", "G", "B",
             "C_cmyk", "M_cmyk", "Y_cmyk", "K_cmyk", "H_hsv", "S_hsv", "V_hsv",
             "L_lab", "a_lab", "b_lab", "C_lch", "h_lch", "family", "coarse_family", "quality", "source"]

def build_workbook(extra_sheets=()):
    wb = Workbook(); ws0 = wb.active; ws0.title = "README"
    notes = ["Colour-of-the-Year database – Claude (Anthropic), David Aguilar, Camila Gómez (2026)",
             "Sheets: Pantone_COTY (target series), Industry_COTY (paint brands, leading indicators),",
             "Decades_1920_2020 (historical literature, approximate HEX), Harmonies (colour-wheel combinations),",
             "Backtest_* (walk-forward model evaluation) and Forecast_2027 (three-option forecast).",
             "Column 'hex' is painted with the real colour. CMYK is a naive conversion (no ICC profile).",
             "CIELAB uses D65 white; colour differences use CIEDE2000.",
             "Sources are listed per row in column 'source'."]
    for n in notes: ws0.append([n])
    ws0.column_dimensions["A"].width = 120
    write_sheet(wb, "Pantone_COTY", pan[CORE_COLS], widths={"name": 18, "source": 60})
    write_sheet(wb, "Industry_COTY", ind.sort_values(["year", "brand"])[CORE_COLS], widths={"name": 20, "brand": 18, "source": 50})
    write_sheet(wb, "Decades_1920_2020", dec[CORE_COLS], widths={"name": 18, "source": 60})
    hm = db[["series", "year", "brand", "name", "hex"] + HARM]
    write_sheet(wb, "Harmonies", hm, swatch_cols=["hex"] + HARM, widths={"name": 20})
    for title, df, sw in extra_sheets:
        write_sheet(wb, title, df, swatch_cols=sw)
    wb.save(f"{DATA_DIR}/color_database.xlsx")

build_workbook()
print("Saved", f"{DATA_DIR}/color_database.xlsx")

A.4 Exploratory analysis¶

A.4.1 The Pantone series as a colour timeline¶

In [6]:
def draw_strip(ax, df, title):
    # One swatch per colour, ordered by year (two-colour years share the column)
    years = sorted(df.year.unique())
    for i, y in enumerate(years):
        sub = df[df.year == y].sort_values("rank")
        n = len(sub)
        for k, (_, r) in enumerate(sub.iterrows()):
            ax.add_patch(mpatches.Rectangle((i, k / n), 0.95, 1 / n, color=r.hex))
            ax.text(i + 0.47, k / n + 0.5 / n, r["name"], rotation=90, ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=6.5, color="#" + _text_color(r.hex))
    ax.set_xlim(0, len(years)); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(years)) + 0.47); ax.set_xticklabels(years, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    for s in ax.spines.values(): s.set_visible(False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 3.2))
draw_strip(ax, pan, "Pantone Colour of the Year, 2000–2026")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{FIG_DIR}/fig1_pantone_timeline.png", bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

A.4.2 The chromatic circle (CIELAB hue × chroma)¶

Angle = CIELAB hue angle h, radius = chroma C*. The arrows follow the Pantone sequence year by year; the faint dots are the paint-industry colours. The background ring shows the hue circle at medium lightness.

In [7]:
def chromatic_circle(ax, df_main, df_bg=None, arrows=True, label=True, ring_L=65, ring_C=45):
    # Background hue ring computed from CIELAB (L=ring_L, C=ring_C) -> sRGB
    for h in range(0, 360, 3):
        ax.bar(math.radians(h + 1.5), 8, width=math.radians(3.1), bottom=88,
               color=lab_to_hex(lch_to_lab((ring_L, ring_C, h))), edgecolor="none")
    if df_bg is not None:
        ax.scatter(np.radians(df_bg.h_lch), df_bg.C_lch, s=28, c=list(df_bg.hex), alpha=0.55,
                   edgecolors="grey", linewidths=0.4, zorder=2)
    d = df_main.sort_values(["year", "rank"])
    if arrows:
        prim = d[d["rank"] == 1]
        for (_, a), (_, b) in zip(prim.iloc[:-1].iterrows(), prim.iloc[1:].iterrows()):
            ax.annotate("", xy=(math.radians(b.h_lch), b.C_lch), xytext=(math.radians(a.h_lch), a.C_lch),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="grey", lw=0.6, alpha=0.6), zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(np.radians(d.h_lch), d.C_lch, s=150, c=list(d.hex), edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.8, zorder=4)
    if label:
        for _, r in d.iterrows():
            ax.text(math.radians(r.h_lch), r.C_lch + 6, str(r.year)[2:], fontsize=7, ha="center", zorder=5)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 96); ax.set_yticks([20, 40, 60, 80]); ax.set_yticklabels(["C*20", "40", "60", "80"], fontsize=7)
    ax.set_rlabel_position(135)
    ax.set_xticks(np.radians(np.arange(0, 360, 30)))
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"{a}°" for a in range(0, 360, 30)], fontsize=7)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6.8))

A.4.3 Is there any temporal structure? (persistence vs. novelty)¶

If the Colour of the Year were persistent, consecutive colours would be closer to each other than random pairs. Fashion theory (Simmel, 1904/1957; Lipovetsky, 1987) predicts the opposite: novelty – each choice moves away from the previous one. We test this with a permutation test on the mean consecutive ΔE₀₀.

In [9]:
def series_labs(df):
    # one Lab vector per year (rank-1 colour) in chronological order
    d = df[df["rank"] == 1].sort_values("year")
    return d.year.values, d[LAB].values

def consecutive_de(labs):
    return np.array([delta_e2000(labs[i], labs[i + 1]) for i in range(len(labs) - 1)])

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
res = []
for nm, df in [("Pantone", pan)] + [(b, ind[ind.brand == b]) for b in CORE_BRANDS]:
    yrs, labs = series_labs(df)
    obs = consecutive_de(labs).mean()
    perm = np.array([consecutive_de(labs[rng.permutation(len(labs))]).mean() for _ in range(5000)])
    lag1 = [stats.pearsonr(df.sort_values("year")[c].values[:-1], df.sort_values("year")[c].values[1:])[0]
            for c in ["L_lab", "a_lab", "b_lab"]]
    res.append({"series": nm, "n_years": len(labs), "mean_consecutive_dE00": round(obs, 2),
                "mean_dE00_random_order": round(perm.mean(), 2),
                "p_value_persistence (obs<perm)": round((perm <= obs).mean(), 3),
                "p_value_novelty (obs>perm)": round((perm >= obs).mean(), 3),
                "lag1_autocorr_L": round(lag1[0], 2), "lag1_autocorr_a": round(lag1[1], 2), "lag1_autocorr_b": round(lag1[2], 2)})
structure = pd.DataFrame(res)
structure

A.4.4 The long series: a century of decade palettes¶

With one observation per decade we cannot forecast years, but we can ask whether lightness and chroma cycle (the "revival" hypothesis, Laver 1937) and how far each decade moves from the previous one.

In [10]:
dec_stats = dec.groupby("year").agg(L_mean=("L_lab", "mean"), C_mean=("C_lch", "mean"), n=("hex", "size")).reset_index()
centroids = dec.groupby("year")[LAB].mean()
dec_stats["dE00_vs_previous_decade"] = [np.nan] + [round(delta_e2000(centroids.iloc[i - 1].values, centroids.iloc[i].values), 2)
                                                    for i in range(1, len(centroids))]
# most similar earlier decade (revival test)
most_sim = [np.nan]
for i in range(1, len(centroids)):
    d = [delta_e2000(centroids.iloc[j].values, centroids.iloc[i].values) for j in range(i)]
    most_sim.append(int(centroids.index[int(np.argmin(d))]))
dec_stats["most_similar_earlier_decade"] = most_sim
dec_stats["gap_decades"] = (dec_stats.year - dec_stats.most_similar_earlier_decade) / 10

# Autocorrelation of mean chroma at lags 1..4 decades (very few points -> descriptive only)
acf_C = {f"lag{k}": round(pd.Series(dec_stats.C_mean).autocorr(k), 2) for k in range(1, 5)}
print("Autocorrelation of decade mean chroma:", acf_C)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.2))
for i, (y, g) in enumerate(dec.groupby("year")):
    for k, (_, r) in enumerate(g.iterrows()):

ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.plot(np.arange(len(dec_stats)) + 0.47, dec_stats.C_mean, "k-o", lw=1.5, label="mean chroma C*")

A.5 Forecasting set-up¶

Target. The Pantone Colour of the Year of year t, represented as a point in CIELAB (L*, a*, b*). Working in a*/b* instead of hue angle avoids the 0°/360° wrap-around problem.

Information set. To forecast year t a model can use (i) Pantone colours up to t−1, and (ii) the paint-industry Colours of the Year for year t (announced August–October, before Pantone's December reveal). Decade palettes are not used as features (different frequency), only as context.

Evaluation. Expanding-window walk-forward back-test: for every year t = 2011…2026 each model is re-trained using only information available at that time and predicts year t (16 genuine out-of-sample forecasts). Metrics:

  • ΔE₀₀ between forecast and actual colour (for two-colour years, the closer of the two counts – a forecast hitting either official colour is a hit);
  • Family accuracy – the forecast falls in the same coarse hue family (Red, Orange/Earth, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple/Pink, Neutral);
  • Random-draw benchmark – the expected ΔE₀₀ of picking one past Pantone colour at random.

Models (17).

# Model Idea
1 Naive (persistence) next = last year
2 Historical mean expanding mean of all past colours
3 Linear trend OLS of each Lab coordinate on year
4 Drift last + average yearly change
5 VAR(1) Lab(t) = A·Lab(t−1) + c, OLS
6 Ridge (lags 1–2) penalised regression on two lags
7 k-NN analogues Lorenz analogue method: what followed the most similar past years
8 Random Forest lags 1–2 + year
9 Gradient Boosting lags 1–2 + year
10 Gaussian Process RBF + white noise kernel on lags
11 Neural network (MLP) 1 hidden layer, 16 units
12 Hue rotation last hue + median signed hue jump, mean L*/C*
13 Max-novelty historical-gamut point farthest from the last 3 colours
14 Industry consensus mean Lab of same-year paint colours
15 Industry, Pantone-style consensus with Pantone's typical lightness/chroma offset
16 Ridge + industry lags + same-year industry consensus
17 Pooled global Ridge lag-1 model trained on Pantone and paint-brand transitions
– Ensemble (mean of all) simple average of the 17 forecasts

# ------------------------- helper data structures ----------------------------
PAN_PRIMARY = pan[pan["rank"] == 1].set_index("year")[LAB]                   # one Lab per year (lags)
PAN_ALL = {y: g[LAB].values for y, g in pan.groupby("year")}                  # all official colours (targets)
CORE = ind[ind.brand.isin(CORE_BRANDS)]
IND_MEAN = CORE.groupby("year")[LAB].mean()                                   # same-year industry consensus

def lch_arr(lab_rows):
    return np.array([lab_to_lch(r) for r in lab_rows])

def training_table(t, lags=(1, 2), with_year=False, with_industry=False):
    # Supervised table using only target years < t. Two-colour years contribute two rows.
    X, Y = [], []
    for y in range(2000, t):
        if y not in PAN_ALL or any((y - l) not in PAN_PRIMARY.index for l in lags): continue
        if with_industry and y not in IND_MEAN.index: continue
        feats = np.concatenate([PAN_PRIMARY.loc[y - l].values for l in lags])
        if with_year: feats = np.append(feats, y)
        if with_industry: feats = np.concatenate([feats, IND_MEAN.loc[y].values])
        for lab in PAN_ALL[y]:
            X.append(feats); Y.append(lab)
    return np.array(X), np.array(Y)

def query_row(t, lags=(1, 2), with_year=False, with_industry=False, ind_override=None):
    feats = np.concatenate([PAN_PRIMARY.loc[t - l].values for l in lags])
    if with_year: feats = np.append(feats, t)
    if with_industry:
        feats = np.concatenate([feats, ind_override if ind_override is not None else IND_MEAN.loc[t].values])
    return feats.reshape(1, -1)

def past_labs(t):
    return np.vstack([PAN_ALL[y] for y in PAN_ALL if y < t])

# Pantone vs. same-year industry: typical lightness/chroma offsets (computed with years < t only)
def pantone_style_offset(t):
    yrs = [y for y in IND_MEAN.index if y < t and y in PAN_PRIMARY.index]
    if len(yrs) < 2: return 0.0, 0.0
    p = lch_arr(PAN_PRIMARY.loc[yrs].values); q = lch_arr(IND_MEAN.loc[yrs].values)
    return float(np.median(p[:, 0] - q[:, 0])), float(np.median(p[:, 1] - q[:, 1]))
In [12]:
# ------------------------------- the models ----------------------------------
def sk_model(estimator, lags=(1, 2), with_year=False, with_industry=False, scale=True):
    # Wrap any scikit-learn regressor into a forecaster f(t) -> Lab
    def f(t, ind_override=None):
        X, Y = training_table(t, lags, with_year, with_industry)
        if len(X) < 4:   # not enough history yet (e.g. industry data start in 2011) -> simple fallback
            return m_industry(t, ind_override) if with_industry else past_labs(t).mean(axis=0)
        est = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), estimator) if scale else estimator
        est.fit(X, Y)
        return est.predict(query_row(t, lags, with_year, with_industry, ind_override))[0]
    return f

def m_naive(t, ind_override=None):  return PAN_PRIMARY.loc[t - 1].values
def m_mean(t, ind_override=None):   return past_labs(t).mean(axis=0)

def m_trend(t, ind_override=None):
    yrs = [y for y in PAN_ALL if y < t for _ in PAN_ALL[y]]
    return LinearRegression().fit(np.array(yrs).reshape(-1, 1), past_labs(t)).predict([[t]])[0]

def m_drift(t, ind_override=None):
    s = PAN_PRIMARY.loc[:t - 1].values
    return s[-1] + (s[-1] - s[0]) / (len(s) - 1)

def m_hue_rotation(t, ind_override=None):
    lch = lch_arr(PAN_PRIMARY.loc[:t - 1].values)
    jumps = (np.diff(lch[:, 2]) + 180) % 360 - 180           # signed circular hue jumps
    h = (lch[-1, 2] + np.median(jumps)) % 360
    return lch_to_lab((lch[:, 0].mean(), lch[:, 1].mean(), h))

def m_max_novelty(t, ind_override=None):
    # Among past Pantone colours (= the plausible gamut), pick the one farthest from the last 3
    cands = past_labs(t)
    recent = [PAN_PRIMARY.loc[y].values for y in range(t - 3, t)]
    score = [min(delta_e2000(c, r) for r in recent) for c in cands]
    return cands[int(np.argmax(score))]

def m_industry(t, ind_override=None):
    return ind_override if ind_override is not None else IND_MEAN.loc[t].values

def m_industry_style(t, ind_override=None):
    L, C, h = lab_to_lch(m_industry(t, ind_override))
    dL, dC = pantone_style_offset(t)
    return lch_to_lab((L + dL, max(C + dC, 0), h))

def m_pooled(t, ind_override=None):
    # 'Global' model: learns lag-1 dynamics from all four series (more training transitions)
    X, Y = [], []
    for nm, df in [("Pantone", pan)] + [(b, CORE[CORE.brand == b]) for b in CORE_BRANDS]:
        s = df[df["rank"] == 1].set_index("year")[LAB]
        for y in s.index:
            if y < t and (y - 1) in s.index:
                X.append(np.append(s.loc[y - 1].values, nm == "Pantone")); Y.append(s.loc[y].values)
    est = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=3.0)).fit(np.array(X), np.array(Y))
    return est.predict(np.append(PAN_PRIMARY.loc[t - 1].values, 1).reshape(1, -1))[0]

GP_KERNEL = ConstantKernel(1.0) * RBF(length_scale=2.0) + WhiteKernel(1.0)
MODELS = {
    "Naive (persistence)":   m_naive,
    "Historical mean":       m_mean,
    "Linear trend":          m_trend,
    "Drift":                 m_drift,
    "VAR(1)":                sk_model(LinearRegression(), lags=(1,), scale=False),
    "Ridge (lags 1-2)":      sk_model(Ridge(alpha=5.0)),
    "k-NN analogues":        sk_model(KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3), lags=(1,)),
    "Random Forest":         sk_model(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=SEED), with_year=True, scale=False),
    "Gradient Boosting":     sk_model(MultiOutputRegressor(GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=150, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=SEED)), with_year=True, scale=False),
    "Gaussian Process":      sk_model(GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=GP_KERNEL, normalize_y=True, random_state=SEED)),
    "Neural net (MLP)":      sk_model(MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(16,), alpha=1.0, max_iter=5000, random_state=SEED)),
    "Hue rotation":          m_hue_rotation,
    "Max-novelty":           m_max_novelty,
    "Industry consensus":    m_industry,
    "Industry, Pantone-style": m_industry_style,
    "Ridge + industry":      sk_model(Ridge(alpha=5.0), lags=(1,), with_industry=True),
    "Pooled global Ridge":   m_pooled,
}
print(len(MODELS), "models defined")

# --------------------------- walk-forward back-test ---------------------------
TEST_YEARS = list(range(2011, 2027))

def score(pred, t):
    # Distance to the closest official colour of year t + family hit
    des = [delta_e2000(pred, a) for a in PAN_ALL[t]]
    j = int(np.argmin(des))
    hit = coarse_family(pred) in {coarse_family(a) for a in PAN_ALL[t]}
    return des[j], hit

records = []
for t in TEST_YEARS:
    preds = {}
    for name, f in MODELS.items():
        preds[name] = np.asarray(f(t), float)
    preds["Ensemble (mean of all)"] = np.mean(list(preds.values()), axis=0)
    rand_de = np.mean([min(delta_e2000(p, a) for a in PAN_ALL[t]) for p in past_labs(t)])
    for name, p in preds.items():
        de, hit = score(p, t)
        records.append({"year": t, "model": name, "pred_hex": lab_to_hex(p), "actual_hex": pan[pan.year == t].hex.iloc[0],
                        "dE00": de, "family_hit": hit, "random_draw_dE00": rand_de,
                        "pred_L": p[0], "pred_a": p[1], "pred_b": p[2]})
bt = pd.DataFrame(records)

def boot_ci(x, n=5000):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    m = [rng.choice(x, len(x)).mean() for _ in range(n)]
    return np.percentile(m, [2.5, 97.5])

naive_de = bt[bt.model == "Naive (persistence)"].set_index("year").dE00
rand_series = bt[bt.model == "Naive (persistence)"].set_index("year").random_draw_dE00
summary = []
for name, g in bt.groupby("model"):
    g = g.set_index("year")
    lo, hi = boot_ci(g.dE00.values)
    # Wilcoxon signed-rank test: is the model better than the random-draw benchmark?
    p_rand = stats.wilcoxon(g.dE00, rand_series, alternative="less").pvalue
    summary.append({"model": name, "mean_dE00": g.dE00.mean(), "CI95_low": lo, "CI95_high": hi,
                    "median_dE00": g.dE00.median(), "family_accuracy": g.family_hit.mean(),
                    "hits_dE<20": int((g.dE00 < 20).sum()),
                    "skill_vs_random_%": 100 * (1 - g.dE00.mean() / rand_series.mean()),
                    "p_better_than_random": p_rand})
summary = pd.DataFrame(summary).sort_values("mean_dE00").reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Random-draw benchmark: mean ΔE00 = {rand_series.mean():.2f} | n forecasts = {len(TEST_YEARS)}")
summary.round(3)

A.5.2 Robustness: does the ranking survive small changes?¶

With only 16 test points, a "winner" can be an artefact. We re-run the back-test on two sub-periods and with different hyper-parameters for the ML models.

A.6 From colour points to colour families: an evidence-fusion classifier¶

The back-test reveals the central problem of point forecasting in colour space: models that minimise ΔE₀₀ converge to the centre of the colour cloud (a muted brownish-pink), which is "never very wrong" but almost never names the right colour family (family accuracy ≤ 38%). The question a designer actually asks is "which family will it be?". We therefore reformulate the problem as a 7-class classification (Red, Orange/Earth, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple/Pink, Neutral) and combine four independent pieces of evidence in a product-of-experts (naive-Bayes-like) score:

Expert What it encodes Estimated from
Base rate how often Pantone chose each family Pantone years < t (Laplace-smoothed)
Novelty Pantone avoids repeating a family used in the previous two years empirical repeat rate, years < t
Industry votes same-year paint Colours of the Year (announced before Pantone) year t industry colours
Model votes families predicted by the 17 walk-forward models the year-t forecasts of section A.5

The three families with the highest posterior score become the three options. Because "one of my three options was right" is exactly what we will claim for 2027, the method is back-tested with top-1 and top-3 accuracy (random guessing: 1/7 = 14% and 3/7 = 43%), together with an ablation of each expert.

In [17]:
FAMS = COARSE_FAMILIES
fam_seq = {y: coarse_family(PAN_PRIMARY.loc[y].values) for y in PAN_PRIMARY.index}
fam_all = {y: {coarse_family(v) for v in PAN_ALL[y]} for y in PAN_ALL}

def expert_base(t):
    cnt = pd.Series([fam_seq[y] for y in fam_seq if y < t]).value_counts()
    v = np.array([cnt.get(f, 0) + 1 for f in FAMS], float)              # Laplace smoothing
    return v / v.sum()

def repeat_rate(t):
    # empirical P(family of year y is one of the families of years y-1, y-2), using years < t
    hits = [fam_seq[y] in {fam_seq[y - 1], fam_seq[y - 2]} for y in fam_seq if y < t and y - 2 in fam_seq]
    return (sum(hits) + 1) / (len(hits) + 2)

def expert_novelty(t):
    recent = {fam_seq[t - 1], fam_seq[t - 2]}
    r = repeat_rate(t)
    v = np.array([r / len(recent) if f in recent else (1 - r) / (len(FAMS) - len(recent)) for f in FAMS])
    return v / v.sum()

def expert_votes(families):
    cnt = pd.Series(list(families)).value_counts() if len(families) else pd.Series(dtype=float)
    v = np.array([cnt.get(f, 0) + 0.5 for f in FAMS], float)            # Jeffreys-type smoothing
    return v / v.sum()

def industry_families(t):
    return [coarse_family(r) for r in CORE[CORE.year == t][LAB].values]

def model_families(t, table=None):
    tab = bt[(bt.year == t) & (bt.model != "Ensemble (mean of all)")] if table is None else table
    return [coarse_family(np.array([r.pred_L, r.pred_a, r.pred_b])) for r in tab.itertuples()]

EXPERT_SETS = {
    "Base rate only":                 ["base"],
    "Novelty only":                   ["novelty"],
    "Industry votes only":            ["industry"],
    "Model votes only":               ["models"],
    "Base × novelty":                 ["base", "novelty"],
    "Base × novelty × industry":      ["base", "novelty", "industry"],
    "Full fusion (all four experts)": ["base", "novelty", "industry", "models"],
}

def fuse(t, experts, ind_fams=None, mod_fams=None):
    parts = {"base": expert_base(t), "novelty": expert_novelty(t),
             "industry": expert_votes(industry_families(t) if ind_fams is None else ind_fams),
             "models": expert_votes(model_families(t) if mod_fams is None else mod_fams)}
    p = np.prod([parts[e] for e in experts], axis=0)
    return pd.Series(p / p.sum(), index=FAMS)

fam_rows = []
for t in TEST_YEARS:
    for nm, ex in EXPERT_SETS.items():
        post = fuse(t, ex).sort_values(ascending=False)
        top = list(post.index)
        fam_rows.append({"year": t, "method": nm, "actual": "/".join(sorted(fam_all[t])), "top3": ", ".join(top[:3]),
                         "top1_hit": top[0] in fam_all[t], "top3_hit": bool(set(top[:3]) & fam_all[t]),
                         "log_score": np.log(max(post[list(fam_all[t])].max(), 1e-9))})
fam_bt = pd.DataFrame(fam_rows)
fam_summary = (fam_bt.groupby("method")[["top1_hit", "top3_hit", "log_score"]].mean()
               .rename(columns={"top1_hit": "top1_accuracy", "top3_hit": "top3_accuracy", "log_score": "mean_log_score"}))
fam_summary["log_score_uniform"] = np.log(1 / 7)
# exact binomial test of the top-3 hit rate against random guessing (3/7)
fam_summary["p_top3_vs_random"] = [stats.binomtest(int(round(a * len(TEST_YEARS))), len(TEST_YEARS), 3 / 7,
                                                   alternative="greater").pvalue for a in fam_summary.top3_accuracy]
fam_summary = fam_summary.loc[list(EXPERT_SETS)]
print("Empirical repeat rate of a family within 2 years (all data):", round(repeat_rate(2027), 2))
fam_summary.round(3)

Calibration. A product of experts that are not independent (e.g. the base rate and the model votes both favour frequent families) is over-confident: the raw full-fusion posterior has a worse log score than a uniform guess even though its top-3 ranking is the best. We therefore temper the posterior, p ∝ posterior^τ, choosing τ to maximise the back-test log score. This uses the back-test years twice (in-sample), so the tempered numbers should be read as indicative.

In [18]:
FULL = EXPERT_SETS["Full fusion (all four experts)"]
posts = {t: fuse(t, FULL) for t in TEST_YEARS}

def mean_log_score(tau):
    out = []
    for t, p in posts.items():
        q = p ** tau; q /= q.sum()
        out.append(np.log(q[list(fam_all[t])].max()))
    return np.mean(out)

taus = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 1.01, 0.05), 2)
ls = [mean_log_score(x) for x in taus]
TAU_CAL = float(taus[int(np.argmax(ls))])
print(f"best temperature tau = {TAU_CAL} | log score {max(ls):.3f} vs uniform {np.log(1/7):.3f} vs raw {mean_log_score(1.0):.3f}")

A.7 Forecast for 2027¶

Leading indicators already available (12 October 2026). Seven paint Colours of the Year 2027 have a published HEX and eight more were announced with a verbal description only (WGSN × Coloro, California Paints, Clark+Kensington, PPG global, Little Greene, Graham & Brown, C2, Minwax). Each announcement is assigned to the family the brand itself declares (e.g. Behr Grounded = "mossy olive green"), which we cross-check against its CIELAB hue.

From family to a concrete colour. For each of the three selected families we build a Pantone-calibrated colour: the hue is the chroma-weighted circular mean of the 2027 industry colours in that family (or, if there are none, the median hue of Pantone's own picks in that family), and lightness/chroma are the medians of Pantone's past picks in that family (Pantone's colours are typically far more chromatic than paint colours – median offset ΔC* ≈ +28). The point is then snapped to the nearest real commercial colour in a library of 11,730 paint colours, so each option is a reproducible, purchasable reference.

# --- make each of the top-3 families concrete ------------------------------------
universe = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/paint_color_universe.csv")
universe_lab = np.vstack([hex_to_lab(h) for h in universe.hex])

def nearest_real_colour(lab):
    # Euclidean pre-filter, then exact CIEDE2000 among the 40 closest library colours
    idx = np.argsort(np.linalg.norm(universe_lab - lab, axis=1))[:40]
    best = min(idx, key=lambda i: delta_e2000(lab, universe_lab[i]))
    return universe.iloc[best], delta_e2000(lab, universe_lab[best])

def circular_mean_deg(angles, weights):
    a = np.radians(angles)
    return math.degrees(math.atan2(np.sum(weights * np.sin(a)), np.sum(weights * np.cos(a)))) % 360

pan_lch = pan.assign(cf=[coarse_family(v) for v in pan[LAB].values])
top3 = list(fusion27.index[:3])
options = []
for k, fam in enumerate(top3, 1):
    members = ind27[ind27.declared_family == fam]
    pf = pan_lch[pan_lch.cf == fam]
    if len(members):
        hue = circular_mean_deg(members.h_lch.values, members.C_lch.values)
        hue_src = "2027 industry colours: " + ", ".join(members.brand + " " + members.name)
    else:
        hue = circular_mean_deg(pf.h_lch.values, pf.C_lch.values)
        hue_src = "median hue of Pantone's past picks in this family"
    L_, C_ = (pf.L_lab.median(), pf.C_lch.median()) if len(pf) >= 2 else (pan.L_lab.median(), pan.C_lch.median())
    target = lch_to_lab((L_, C_, hue))

A.8 Critique of the models and of the method¶

What the evidence supports

  • Pantone's sequence is not random and not persistent: consecutive colours are further apart than chance (permutation p ≈ 0.02). Paint brands behave the opposite way (slow, persistent drift). This "novelty rule" is the single most useful regularity found.
  • Combining base rates, novelty and the paint brands' early announcements identifies a short list of three families that contained the real Pantone family in 12 of 16 back-test years (75%, binomial p ≈ 0.01 vs. 43% by chance).

What it does not support

  1. ML does not beat simple statistics here. The best point models (pooled Ridge, ensemble, historical mean) are statistically indistinguishable (overlapping bootstrap CIs), and the historical mean is as good as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting or a Gaussian Process. With 27 observations, flexible models (MLP, k-NN with k = 1) overfit, exactly as reported in large forecasting competitions (Makridakis et al., 2018).
  2. The ΔE-optimal forecast is a trap. Minimising colour distance pulls every model towards the centre of the colour cloud – a muddy brownish-pink that is never chosen. Low ΔE ≠ correct colour. The family-level reformulation is more honest but discards shade information.
  3. Unstable rankings. The Spearman correlation between model ranks in 2011–2018 and 2019–2026 is only ≈ 0.5; Ridge (lags 1–2) goes from 1st to 13th. Any "best model" claim based on 16 test points is fragile, and choosing the winner by back-test is itself a form of over-fitting.
  4. The target is a curatorial decision, not a natural process. Pantone's choice is made by a committee reacting to culture, marketing and possibly to the very forecasts published by others. Past colours explain little; exogenous drivers (economy, technology, social mood) are not in the data.
  5. Measurement issues. HEX values are sRGB approximations of physical TCX/paint standards; different official sources differ by up to ΔE ≈ 5 (e.g. Viva Magenta). Two-colour years (2016, 2021) and the nine-colour Sherwin-Williams 2025 capsule required ad-hoc rules.
  6. Leading indicators are few and noisy. Only 1–3 paint brands per year have a full history; the 2027 vote mixes HEX-coded and verbally described colours, and brands may imitate each other (non-independent votes). Benjamin Moore's 2027 colour was not yet known.
  7. Over-confidence of the fusion. The experts are not independent, so the raw posterior is over-confident (log score worse than uniform). Temperature scaling fixes this only in-sample (τ fitted on the same 16 years).
  8. The long series is weak. Decade palettes are literature-based, approximate, and one point per decade; they show no regular revival cycle and cannot be used for year-ahead prediction.
  9. Hand-made choices. Family boundaries, the "Brown/Earth" rule, smoothing constants and the declared families of 2027 announcements are researcher choices; different choices would move the probabilities.

How to improve: (i) add exogenous yearly covariates (Google Trends of colour names, runway colour shares from WGSN/Tagwalk, macro-economic mood indices); (ii) collect more parallel series (WGSN/Coloro, Dulux, Valspar, PPG histories) to train a genuine panel model; (iii) treat the problem as probabilistic classification with proper scoring rules from the start; (iv) pre-register the 2027 forecast (this notebook, committed to GitHub before December 2026) and evaluate it when Pantone announces.

Part B — Paper (English)¶

Can machine learning forecast the Colour of the Year? Evidence from Pantone 2000–2026, paint-industry leading indicators and a 2027 three-option forecast¶

Claudea,*, David Aguilarb, Camila Gómezb

a Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA  ·  b [Affiliation to be completed]

* Lead author.

Preprint — 12 October 2026. Code and data: this repository.

Highlights

  • A 145-record colour database (Pantone, paint brands, decade palettes) in HEX, RGB, CMYK, HSV, CIELAB.
  • Pantone colours are anti-persistent: each pick moves away from the previous one (p ≈ 0.02).
  • Seventeen forecasting models: none clearly beats the historical mean in CIEDE2000 error.
  • An evidence-fusion classifier put the true family in its top three in 12 of 16 years.
  • For 2027 we forecast Earth/terracotta (≈31%), Blue (≈21%) or olive Green (≈14%).

Keywords: colour forecasting · Colour of the Year · time series · machine learning · CIEDE2000 · fashion cycles

Abstract¶

Every December Pantone announces a "Colour of the Year" that influences fashion, product and graphic design. We ask whether this choice can be forecast from its own history. We assembled a database of the 29 Pantone colours of 2000–2026, 45 paint-industry Colours of the Year (Sherwin-Williams, Benjamin Moore, Behr and seven 2027 announcements) and 71 decade-level colours for the 1920s–2020s, each described in sRGB, CMYK, HSV and CIELAB. A permutation test shows that Pantone's sequence is anti-persistent: consecutive colours differ by a mean ΔE₀₀ of 41.5 versus 36.2 for random orderings (p = 0.023), whereas paint brands drift persistently. Seventeen models — naive, mean, trend, VAR, Ridge, k-nearest analogues, random forest, gradient boosting, Gaussian process, neural network, hue-rotation, novelty and industry-consensus models, and a pooled global model — were evaluated by an expanding-window walk-forward back-test over 2011–2026. The best models reduce colour error by about 28% relative to a random historical draw (mean ΔE₀₀ ≈ 25 vs 35.6) but are statistically indistinguishable from the historical mean, and their forecasts collapse towards the centre of colour space. Reformulating the task as a seven-family classification and fusing four experts (base rate, novelty, same-year industry votes and model votes) placed the correct family among the top three in 75% of the back-test years (random: 43%; p = 0.009). Using fifteen 2027 announcements already public, the method forecasts for Pantone 2027: (1) a terracotta Orange/Earth tone, #C76C4C (calibrated probability ≈ 31%); (2) a clear mid Blue, #69B2CC (≈ 21%); (3) an olive Yellow-Green, #9A9C49 (≈ 14%). We discuss why machine learning offers limited gains on a 27-point curatorial series and how the forecast can be falsified in December 2026.

1. Introduction¶

Since 2000, the Pantone Color Institute has selected an annual "Colour of the Year" (COTY) that is widely adopted by fashion, cosmetics, interior and graphic design. Paint manufacturers followed with their own selections (Sherwin-Williams since 2011, Benjamin Moore since 2012, Behr since 2018). These choices are made by expert committees, but they are also data: a short, annual, multivariate time series of colours.

Three questions motivate this paper. (Q1) Does the Pantone sequence contain temporal structure — persistence, trend, cycles or novelty? (Q2) Can statistical and machine-learning (ML) models forecast next year's colour better than chance, and which ones? (Q3) Given the information available on 12 October 2026, what are the most likely candidates for the Pantone Colour of the Year 2027?

Our contributions are: (i) an open, auditable database of 145 colours with full colour-space descriptions and colour-wheel harmonies, delivered as an Excel workbook with painted swatches; (ii) a rigorous walk-forward comparison of 17 forecasting models using the CIEDE2000 metric; (iii) a family-level evidence-fusion classifier that exploits the paint industry's earlier announcements; and (iv) a pre-registered, falsifiable three-option forecast for 2027.

2. Background¶

Fashion cycles. Sociological theories explain fashion as a dynamic of imitation and distinction that drives continuous novelty (Simmel, 1957; Lipovetsky, 1994). Quantitative studies of dress found long, quasi-regular cycles in silhouettes (Kroeber, 1919; Lowe & Lowe, 1982), and Laver (1937) proposed that styles return after roughly 20–30 years. Colour forecasting is a professional practice built on expert panels and trend research rather than statistics (Diane & Cassidy, 2005); historical overviews describe characteristic palettes by decade (Eiseman & Recker, 2011).

Computational forecasting of style. Al-Halah et al. (2017) forecast the popularity of visual fashion styles from large image collections. Studies of forecasting competitions show that, on short series, simple methods are hard to beat and that ML models frequently overfit (Makridakis et al., 2018). Forecast combination (Bates & Granger, 1969) and products of experts (Hinton, 2002) are standard ways to merge heterogeneous signals.

Colour difference. Euclidean distances in sRGB are not perceptually meaningful. We work in CIELAB (D65) and measure errors with CIEDE2000 (Luo et al., 2001), validated against the test data of Sharma et al. (2005). As a guide, ΔE₀₀ ≈ 1 is a just-noticeable difference and ΔE₀₀ > 30 typically indicates a different colour family.

3. Data¶

Series Period Records Role Source of HEX
Pantone COTY 2000–2026 29 (27 years; two colours in 2016 and 2021) target W3Schools Pantone table, cross-checked with Pantone releases
Sherwin-Williams 2011–2027 16 (2025 "capsule" excluded) leading indicator brand library (colornerd dataset)
Benjamin Moore 2012–2026 15 leading indicator brand library
Behr 2019–2027 9 leading indicator brand library / behr.com
Other 2027 announcements 2027 5 with HEX + 8 verbal 2027 votes brand press, trackers
Decade palettes 1920s–2020s 71 long-memory context standard named-colour values (approximate)

Each colour was converted to RGB, naive CMYK, HSV/HSL, CIELAB and LCh, assigned to one of 13 fine hue families (CIELAB hue sectors calibrated to colour names, plus Neutral and Brown/Earth rules) and seven coarse families, and complemented with complementary, analogous, triadic and split-complementary harmonies. The longest validated annual series is Pantone's (27 years); paint series are shorter, and no annual, coded series of "fashion colours" before 2000 was found. Decade palettes extend the record to the 1920s, but at decadal resolution and with approximate codes.

Fig. 1. Pantone Colours of the Year, 2000–2026.

Fig. 2. Left: the Pantone path on the CIELAB chromatic circle (angle = hue, radius = chroma); faint dots are paint-brand colours. Right: decade palettes 1920s–2020s.

4. Methods¶

4.1 Structure tests. For each series we compared the mean ΔE₀₀ between consecutive colours with its distribution under 5,000 random permutations of the order (one-sided tests for persistence and novelty), and computed lag-1 autocorrelations of L*, a*, b*.

4.2 Point-forecast models. The target is the CIELAB vector of year t. Seventeen models were compared: (1) naive persistence; (2) expanding historical mean; (3) linear trend; (4) drift; (5) VAR(1) by OLS; (6) Ridge regression on lags 1–2; (7) k-nearest-neighbour analogues (Lorenz, 1969); (8) random forest (Breiman, 2001) and (9) gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001) on lags and year; (10) Gaussian-process regression with RBF + white-noise kernel (Rasmussen & Williams, 2006); (11) a one-hidden-layer neural network; (12) hue rotation by the median signed hue jump; (13) maximum novelty with respect to the last three colours; (14) same-year paint-industry consensus; (15) consensus shifted by Pantone's median lightness/chroma offset; (16) Ridge with lags and industry consensus; (17) a pooled "global" Ridge trained on transitions of all four series. All ML models use scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) with fixed seeds.

4.3 Evaluation. Expanding-window walk-forward back-test for t = 2011…2026 (16 forecasts), training only on information available before Pantone's December announcement (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021). Metrics: ΔE₀₀ to the nearest official colour of year t; coarse-family accuracy; skill relative to a random draw from past Pantone colours; bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests against the random benchmark; rank stability across sub-periods and hyper-parameter sensitivity.

4.4 Evidence-fusion classifier. Each year receives a probability over seven coarse families from the product of four experts: a Laplace-smoothed base rate; a novelty prior that gives families used in the previous two years the empirical repeat probability (≈ 0.11); the industry votes of same-year paint colours; and the model votes of the 17 point forecasts. Experts and their ablations were evaluated with top-1/top-3 accuracy and the logarithmic score (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). Because the experts are not independent, the posterior was tempered (p ∝ posterior^τ, τ = 0.35 chosen by back-test log score; Guo et al., 2017).

4.5 From family to colour. For each of the three most probable families, the hue is the chroma-weighted circular mean of the 2027 industry colours of that family, and lightness and chroma are the medians of Pantone's own past choices in that family. The result is snapped to the nearest of 11,730 commercial paint colours (ΔE₀₀ < 3) to provide a reproducible reference.

5. Results¶

5.1 Pantone is anti-persistent. Consecutive Pantone colours are on average ΔE₀₀ = 41.5 apart, versus 36.2 under random ordering (p = 0.023 for novelty); the lag-1 autocorrelation of b* is −0.55 (yellow–blue alternation). Paint brands show the opposite tendency (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 27 vs 30–33; novelty p ≥ 0.83). Decade palettes show the smallest change between the 1960s and 1970s (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 9) and the largest into the 1980s (≈ 33); the most similar earlier decade is 1–9 decades back, with no regular revival period.

5.2 Point forecasts. Table 1 summarises the back-test.

Ten of the 17 models (plus the ensemble) are significantly better than a random draw (Wilcoxon p < 0.05), but their confidence intervals overlap almost entirely, and the historical mean is as accurate as any ML model. Persistence and drift are the worst models, consistent with §5.1. Rankings are unstable (Spearman ρ = 0.49 between 2011–2018 and 2019–2026), and the neural network overfits under every configuration tried (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 34).

The full fusion contained the correct family in its top three in 12 of 16 years. Its top-1 accuracy (19%) is only modestly above chance, and the raw posterior is over-confident (log score −2.21 vs −1.95 for a uniform guess); after tempering, the log score improves to −1.85.

6. Forecast for 2027¶

By 12 October 2026 fifteen 2027 colours had been announced: seven Orange/Earth (e.g. Dutch Boy Deep Rooted, Dunn-Edwards French Press Coffee, PPG Country Soil), five Blue (Valspar Cottage Door, Glidden Artifact, WGSN × Coloro Luminous Blue, …) and three Green (Sherwin-Williams Celery, Behr Grounded, Dulux Soulful Sage). The skill-weighted point forecast of the 17 models is a muted brown (#A7816C). The novelty prior penalises Orange/Earth (Pantone 2025 was Mocha Mousse) and Neutral (2026 was Cloud Dancer), but the industry and model votes outweigh it.

Fig. 5. Recent Pantone path, 2027 paint signals and the three options on the chromatic circle.

The three options jointly carry ≈ 67% of the calibrated probability, in line with the 75% back-test hit rate. Falsification criterion: the forecast is counted as correct if Pantone's 2027 colour belongs to one of the three families; it is counted as precise if its ΔE₀₀ to the corresponding option is below 20.

7. Discussion and limitations¶

The main finding is negative for machine learning and positive for structure. On a 27-point curatorial series, flexible ML models provide no measurable advantage over the historical mean, and ΔE-optimal forecasts converge to an uninformative central colour. What is forecastable is coarse: Pantone rarely repeats the family of the previous two years (≈ 11% of the time), and paint brands, which announce months earlier, carry some information about the family Pantone will choose.

Limitations include: (i) tiny sample and short test window (16 forecasts), so all p-values are fragile and the ranking of models changes between sub-periods; (ii) selecting the best model on the back-test is itself over-fitting; (iii) Pantone's choice is an institutional decision influenced by marketing, culture and possibly by competitors' announcements, none of which are modelled; (iv) HEX values are approximations of physical standards and differ between sources by up to ΔE₀₀ ≈ 5; (v) industry votes are not independent and their 2027 families were partly coded from verbal descriptions; (vi) the temperature parameter was fitted in-sample; (vii) decade palettes are approximate and too coarse for annual prediction; and (viii) family boundaries and smoothing constants are researcher choices.

Future work should add exogenous signals (search trends, runway colour shares, economic sentiment), gather more parallel series to estimate panel models, and evaluate forecasts prospectively with proper scoring rules.

8. Conclusions¶

Pantone's Colour of the Year is anti-persistent and only weakly predictable from its own past. Seventeen models reduce colour error by at most ~28% relative to a random draw and do not beat the historical mean. A transparent fusion of base rates, novelty and paint-industry leading indicators produces useful short lists (top-3 hit rate 75%). For 2027 the method points to a terracotta Orange/Earth (#C76C4C), a clear Blue (#69B2CC) or an olive Green (#9A9C49). Pantone's announcement in December 2026 will provide an out-of-sample test.

Parte C — Artículo (Español)¶

¿Puede el aprendizaje automático pronosticar el Color del Año? Evidencia de Pantone 2000–2026, indicadores adelantados de la industria de pinturas y un pronóstico de tres opciones para 2027¶

Claudea,*, David Aguilarb, Camila Gómezb

a Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, EE. UU.  ·  b [Afiliación por completar]

* Autor principal.

Preprint — 12 de octubre de 2026. Código y datos: este repositorio.

Aspectos destacados

  • Base de 145 colores (Pantone, marcas de pintura, paletas por década) en HEX, RGB, CMYK, HSV y CIELAB.
  • Los colores Pantone son antipersistentes: cada elección se aleja de la anterior (p ≈ 0,02).
  • Diecisiete modelos de pronóstico: ninguno supera con claridad a la media histórica en error CIEDE2000.
  • Un clasificador de fusión de evidencia acertó la familia en su top 3 en 12 de 16 años.
  • Para 2027 pronosticamos Tierra/terracota (≈31 %), Azul (≈21 %) o Verde oliva (≈14 %).

Palabras clave: pronóstico de color · Color del Año · series de tiempo · aprendizaje automático · CIEDE2000 · ciclos de la moda

Resumen¶

Cada diciembre Pantone anuncia un "Color del Año" que influye en la moda, el diseño de producto y el diseño gráfico. Nos preguntamos si esa elección puede pronosticarse a partir de su propia historia. Construimos una base de datos con los 29 colores Pantone de 2000–2026, 45 Colores del Año de la industria de pinturas (Sherwin-Williams, Benjamin Moore, Behr y siete anuncios de 2027) y 71 colores por década de los años 1920 a 2020, cada uno descrito en sRGB, CMYK, HSV y CIELAB. Una prueba de permutación muestra que la serie de Pantone es antipersistente: los colores consecutivos difieren en un ΔE₀₀ medio de 41,5 frente a 36,2 en órdenes aleatorios (p = 0,023), mientras que las marcas de pintura derivan de forma persistente. Se evaluaron diecisiete modelos —ingenuo, media, tendencia, VAR, Ridge, análogos k-vecinos, bosque aleatorio, gradient boosting, proceso gaussiano, red neuronal, rotación de tono, novedad, consenso industrial y un modelo global agrupado— mediante un back-test de ventana creciente (walk-forward) en 2011–2026. Los mejores modelos reducen el error de color cerca de 28 % frente a una elección histórica al azar (ΔE₀₀ medio ≈ 25 frente a 35,6), pero son estadísticamente indistinguibles de la media histórica y sus pronósticos colapsan hacia el centro del espacio de color. Al reformular la tarea como clasificación en siete familias y fusionar cuatro expertos (frecuencia base, novedad, votos de la industria del mismo año y votos de los modelos), la familia correcta quedó entre las tres primeras en el 75 % de los años del back-test (azar: 43 %; p = 0,009). Con quince anuncios de 2027 ya públicos, el método pronostica para Pantone 2027: (1) un tono terracota Naranja/Tierra, #C76C4C (probabilidad calibrada ≈ 31 %); (2) un Azul medio y claro, #69B2CC (≈ 21 %); (3) un Verde-amarillo oliva, #9A9C49 (≈ 14 %). Discutimos por qué el aprendizaje automático aporta poco en una serie curatorial de 27 puntos y cómo el pronóstico podrá refutarse en diciembre de 2026.

1. Introducción¶

Desde 2000, el Pantone Color Institute selecciona cada año un "Color del Año" (COTY) que adoptan ampliamente la moda, la cosmética, el interiorismo y el diseño gráfico. Los fabricantes de pintura siguieron con sus propias selecciones (Sherwin-Williams desde 2011, Benjamin Moore desde 2012, Behr desde 2018). Estas elecciones las hacen comités de expertos, pero también son datos: una serie de tiempo anual, corta y multivariada de colores.

Tres preguntas motivan este artículo. (P1) ¿Contiene la secuencia de Pantone estructura temporal —persistencia, tendencia, ciclos o novedad? (P2) ¿Pueden los modelos estadísticos y de aprendizaje automático (ML) pronosticar el color del año siguiente mejor que el azar, y cuáles? (P3) Con la información disponible el 12 de octubre de 2026, ¿cuáles son los candidatos más probables para el Color del Año Pantone 2027?

Nuestras contribuciones son: (i) una base de datos abierta y auditable de 145 colores con descripción completa en espacios de color y armonías del círculo cromático, entregada como libro de Excel con muestras de color pintadas; (ii) una comparación rigurosa walk-forward de 17 modelos usando la métrica CIEDE2000; (iii) un clasificador de familias por fusión de evidencia que aprovecha los anuncios anticipados de la industria de pinturas; y (iv) un pronóstico pre-registrado y refutable de tres opciones para 2027.

2. Antecedentes¶

Ciclos de la moda. Las teorías sociológicas explican la moda como una dinámica de imitación y distinción que impulsa la novedad continua (Simmel, 1957; Lipovetsky, 1994). Estudios cuantitativos del vestido hallaron ciclos largos y casi regulares en las siluetas (Kroeber, 1919; Lowe y Lowe, 1982), y Laver (1937) propuso que los estilos regresan tras unos 20–30 años. El pronóstico de color es una práctica profesional basada en paneles de expertos e investigación de tendencias más que en estadística (Diane y Cassidy, 2005); las revisiones históricas describen paletas características por década (Eiseman y Recker, 2011).

Pronóstico computacional del estilo. Al-Halah et al. (2017) pronosticaron la popularidad de estilos visuales de moda a partir de grandes colecciones de imágenes. Los estudios de competencias de pronóstico muestran que, en series cortas, los métodos simples son difíciles de superar y que los modelos de ML se sobreajustan con frecuencia (Makridakis et al., 2018). La combinación de pronósticos (Bates y Granger, 1969) y los productos de expertos (Hinton, 2002) son formas estándar de fusionar señales heterogéneas.

Diferencia de color. Las distancias euclidianas en sRGB no tienen significado perceptual. Trabajamos en CIELAB (D65) y medimos errores con CIEDE2000 (Luo et al., 2001), validado con los datos de prueba de Sharma et al. (2005). Como guía, ΔE₀₀ ≈ 1 es una diferencia apenas perceptible y ΔE₀₀ > 30 suele indicar una familia de color distinta.

3. Datos¶

Cada color se convirtió a RGB, CMYK ingenuo, HSV/HSL, CIELAB y LCh; se asignó a una de 13 familias finas de tono (sectores de tono CIELAB calibrados con nombres de color, más reglas de Neutro y Marrón/Tierra) y a siete familias gruesas; y se complementó con sus armonías complementaria, análoga, triádica y complementaria dividida. La serie anual validada más larga es la de Pantone (27 años); las series de pintura son más cortas y no se encontró ninguna serie anual codificada de "colores de moda" anterior a 2000. Las paletas por década extienden el registro hasta los años veinte, pero con resolución decenal y códigos aproximados.

Fig. 1. Colores del Año Pantone, 2000–2026.

Fig. 2. Izquierda: recorrido de Pantone en el círculo cromático CIELAB (ángulo = tono, radio = croma); los puntos tenues son colores de marcas de pintura. Derecha: paletas por década 1920–2020.

4. Métodos¶

4.1 Pruebas de estructura. Para cada serie comparamos el ΔE₀₀ medio entre colores consecutivos con su distribución bajo 5.000 permutaciones aleatorias del orden (pruebas unilaterales de persistencia y novedad), y calculamos las autocorrelaciones de rezago 1 de L*, a*, b*.

4.2 Modelos de pronóstico puntual. El objetivo es el vector CIELAB del año t. Se compararon diecisiete modelos: (1) persistencia ingenua; (2) media histórica creciente; (3) tendencia lineal; (4) deriva; (5) VAR(1) por MCO; (6) regresión Ridge con rezagos 1–2; (7) análogos por k vecinos más cercanos (Lorenz, 1969); (8) bosque aleatorio (Breiman, 2001) y (9) gradient boosting (Friedman, 2001) con rezagos y año; (10) regresión por proceso gaussiano con núcleo RBF + ruido blanco (Rasmussen y Williams, 2006); (11) una red neuronal de una capa oculta; (12) rotación de tono según el salto de tono mediano con signo; (13) máxima novedad respecto de los tres últimos colores; (14) consenso de la industria de pinturas del mismo año; (15) consenso desplazado por la diferencia mediana de luminosidad/croma de Pantone; (16) Ridge con rezagos y consenso industrial; (17) un Ridge "global" agrupado entrenado con las transiciones de las cuatro series. Todos los modelos de ML usan scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) con semillas fijas.

4.3 Evaluación. Back-test walk-forward de ventana creciente para t = 2011…2026 (16 pronósticos), entrenando solo con información disponible antes del anuncio de Pantone en diciembre (Hyndman y Athanasopoulos, 2021). Métricas: ΔE₀₀ al color oficial más cercano del año t; acierto de familia gruesa; habilidad relativa frente a una elección al azar entre colores Pantone pasados; intervalos de confianza bootstrap al 95 %; pruebas de rangos con signo de Wilcoxon frente al referente aleatorio; estabilidad del ranking entre subperiodos y sensibilidad a hiperparámetros.

4.4 Clasificador por fusión de evidencia. Cada año recibe una probabilidad sobre siete familias gruesas a partir del producto de cuatro expertos: una frecuencia base suavizada de Laplace; un previo de novedad que asigna a las familias usadas en los dos años anteriores la probabilidad empírica de repetición (≈ 0,11); los votos de la industria de los colores de pintura del mismo año; y los votos de los modelos de los 17 pronósticos puntuales. Los expertos y sus ablaciones se evaluaron con acierto top-1/top-3 y la puntuación logarítmica (Gneiting y Raftery, 2007). Como los expertos no son independientes, la posterior se templó (p ∝ posterior^τ, τ = 0,35 elegido por la puntuación logarítmica del back-test; Guo et al., 2017).

4.5 De la familia al color. Para cada una de las tres familias más probables, el tono es la media circular ponderada por croma de los colores de la industria 2027 de esa familia, y la luminosidad y el croma son las medianas de las elecciones pasadas de Pantone en esa familia. El resultado se ajusta al más cercano de 11.730 colores comerciales de pintura (ΔE₀₀ < 3) para dar una referencia reproducible.

5. Resultados¶

5.1 Pantone es antipersistente. Los colores Pantone consecutivos distan en promedio ΔE₀₀ = 41,5, frente a 36,2 con orden aleatorio (p = 0,023 para novedad); la autocorrelación de rezago 1 de b* es −0,55 (alternancia amarillo–azul). Las marcas de pintura muestran la tendencia opuesta (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 27 frente a 30–33; p de novedad ≥ 0,83). Las paletas por década muestran el menor cambio entre los sesenta y los setenta (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 9) y el mayor hacia los ochenta (≈ 33); la década anterior más parecida está entre 1 y 9 décadas atrás, sin un periodo regular de "revival".

5.2 Pronósticos puntuales. La Tabla 1 resume el back-test.

Tabla 1. Back-test walk-forward 2011–2026 (16 pronósticos). Menor ΔE₀₀ es mejor; elección al azar = 35,6.

Modelo ΔE₀₀ medio IC 95 % Acierto familia Habilidad vs azar
Ridge global agrupado 25,3 21,1–29,9 0,19 +29 %
Ensamble (media de todos) 25,6 21,1–30,2 0,38 +28 %

Ridge (rezagos 1–2) 25,8 20,8–31,0 0,19 +28 %
Proceso gaussiano 26,5 21,5–31,7 0,25 +25 %

VAR(1) 27,9 21,8–34,2 0,25 +21 %

Diez de los 17 modelos (más el ensamble) son significativamente mejores que una elección al azar (Wilcoxon p < 0,05), pero sus intervalos de confianza se solapan casi por completo, y la media histórica es tan precisa como cualquier modelo de ML. La persistencia y la deriva son los peores modelos, en coherencia con §5.1. Los rankings son inestables (ρ de Spearman = 0,49 entre 2011–2018 y 2019–2026), y la red neuronal se sobreajusta en todas las configuraciones probadas (ΔE₀₀ ≈ 34).

La fusión completa incluyó la familia correcta entre sus tres primeras en 12 de 16 años. Su acierto top-1 (19 %) apenas supera al azar, y la posterior sin templar es demasiado confiada (puntuación logarítmica −2,21 frente a −1,95 de una apuesta uniforme); tras templarla, mejora a −1,85.

6. Pronóstico para 2027¶

Al 12 de octubre de 2026 se habían anunciado quince colores 2027: siete Naranja/Tierra (p. ej., Dutch Boy Deep Rooted, Dunn-Edwards French Press Coffee, PPG Country Soil), cinco Azules (Valspar Cottage Door, Glidden Artifact, WGSN × Coloro Luminous Blue, …) y tres Verdes (Sherwin-Williams Celery, Behr Grounded, Dulux Soulful Sage). El pronóstico puntual ponderado por habilidad de los 17 modelos es un marrón apagado (#A7816C). El previo de novedad penaliza Naranja/Tierra (Pantone 2025 fue Mocha Mousse) y Neutro (2026 fue Cloud Dancer), pero los votos de la industria y de los modelos pesan más.

Tabla 3. Color del Año Pantone 2027: pronóstico de tres opciones (pre-registrado el 12 de octubre de 2026).

Fig. 4. Las tres opciones con sus armonías complementaria, análogas y triádicas.

Fig. 5. Recorrido reciente de Pantone, señales de pintura 2027 y las tres opciones en el círculo cromático.

Las tres opciones suman ≈ 67 % de la probabilidad calibrada, en línea con el 75 % de acierto del back-test. Criterio de refutación: el pronóstico se considera correcto si el color Pantone 2027 pertenece a una de las tres familias, y preciso si su ΔE₀₀ con la opción correspondiente es menor que 20.

7. Discusión y limitaciones¶

El hallazgo principal es negativo para el aprendizaje automático y positivo para la estructura. En una serie curatorial de 27 puntos, los modelos flexibles de ML no aportan ventaja medible sobre la media histórica, y los pronósticos óptimos en ΔE convergen a un color central poco informativo. Lo que sí es pronosticable es grueso: Pantone rara vez repite la familia de los dos años anteriores (≈ 11 % de las veces), y las marcas de pintura, que anuncian meses antes, contienen algo de información sobre la familia que elegirá Pantone.

Las limitaciones incluyen: (i) muestra diminuta y ventana de prueba corta (16 pronósticos), por lo que todos los valores p son frágiles y el ranking de modelos cambia entre subperiodos; (ii) elegir el mejor modelo con el back-test es en sí mismo sobreajuste; (iii) la elección de Pantone es una decisión institucional influida por el marketing, la cultura y posiblemente por los anuncios de la competencia, nada de lo cual se modela; (iv) los valores HEX son aproximaciones de estándares físicos y difieren entre fuentes hasta en ΔE₀₀ ≈ 5; (v) los votos de la industria no son independientes y sus familias 2027 se codificaron en parte a partir de descripciones verbales; (vi) el parámetro de temperatura se ajustó dentro de la muestra; (vii) las paletas por década son aproximadas y demasiado gruesas para la predicción anual; y (viii) los límites de familia y las constantes de suavizado son decisiones de los investigadores.

El trabajo futuro debería añadir señales exógenas (tendencias de búsqueda, participación de colores en pasarelas, sentimiento económico), reunir más series paralelas para estimar modelos de panel y evaluar los pronósticos de forma prospectiva con reglas de puntuación propias.

8. Conclusiones¶

El Color del Año de Pantone es antipersistente y solo débilmente predecible a partir de su propio pasado. Diecisiete modelos reducen el error de color como máximo ~28 % frente a una elección al azar y no superan a la media histórica. Una fusión transparente de frecuencias base, novedad e indicadores adelantados de la industria de pinturas produce listas cortas útiles (acierto top-3 del 75 %). Para 2027 el método apunta a un Naranja/Tierra terracota (#C76C4C), un Azul claro (#69B2CC) o un Verde oliva (#9A9C49). El anuncio de Pantone en diciembre de 2026 será la prueba fuera de muestra.
